p.x:
Last summer, I went to my first music festival with my cousins. There were three stages with rock and pop bands. The music was very loud, and the drums were so powerful that I could feel them in my chest!
On the second day, it rained a lot. Everything was covered in mud, but nobody cared. I was happy I had my raincoat. We danced in the rain and sang all the songs.
At night, the stage lights were beautiful: red, blue and green. Before we went home, I bought a festival T-shirt. I can't wait to go again next year!

Going to a festival soon? Here's some advice.
Tickets: Big festivals are often sold out months before, so buy early, and only from the official website.
What to bring: In Thailand, it can be hot or rainy, so bring a hat and wellies if the ground is wet. Earplugs are important, too. The speakers at the main stage are huge, and loud music can damage your hearing. Bring a reusable cup; many festivals now give a discount if you use one.
At the festival: You'll get a wristband when you arrive; don't lose it! Check the line-up and the setlist times so you don't miss the headliner. If the volume is too high, stand further back from the sound system.
Food and fun: There are usually lots of food trucks, so you won't go hungry. You can also buy merchandise like T-shirts and posters. Some festivals have a jazz tent, an electronic music stage and small gigs in the evening.
Safety: Find the first aid tent when you arrive, and agree on a meeting place with your friends. If you're lucky, you might even meet the band backstage! Enjoy the performance, and if it's good, shout for an encore!

For the audience, a music festival is a few days of euphoric escape. For the organisers, it is a year-long challenge of logistics. Every detail, from transport and water supplies to toilets and waste collection, must be planned for tens of thousands of people.
Safety is the greatest responsibility. Each venue has a maximum capacity, and organisers must manage how people enter, move and leave. When too many people push towards a stage, a crush can occur, and in the worst cases a stampede has led to deaths. Modern festivals therefore use barriers, trained stewards and real-time crowd monitoring. Some have banned crowd surfing, and medical teams watch the mosh pit closely, where energetic fans push and jump into each other.
Behind the stage, a large team works almost invisibly. Roadies transport and set up equipment, sometimes working through the night, while sound engineers run a soundcheck hours before each band performs to make sure everything works perfectly.
Ticketing has become another major issue. Scalpers use software to buy huge numbers of tickets the moment they go on sale, then sell them at inflated prices. In response, some countries have restricted resale or capped prices, and festivals increasingly use name-linked digital tickets. Despite these challenges, the festival industry continues to grow, suggesting that, for many people, the shared experience of live music remains irreplaceable.
